disclaimer: These guides are general self-help information, not medical advice or a substitute for professional care. If you feel unsafe or are thinking about harming yourself, contact emergency services or a crisis line right away.

topics.title: Anxiety
topics.intro: Anxiety is the body's alarm system going off when there is no real emergency. These skills calm the alarm and, over time, retrain it.

topics.title: Low mood & depression
topics.intro: Depression makes everything feel heavy and pointless. These skills work by taking very small steps first; action comes before motivation, not after.

topics.title: Sleep
topics.intro: Sleep problems feed both anxiety and low mood. These habits help most people within a few weeks.

topics.title: Stress & burnout
topics.intro: Long-term overload drains you gradually. Recovery needs rest, boundaries and small restorations, not just a weekend off.

guides.title: Slow breathing to calm your body
guides.summary: A quick way to lower physical anxiety symptoms like a racing heart.
steps: Sit comfortably and rest one hand on your belly.
Breathe in gently through your nose for about 4 seconds, letting your belly rise.
Breathe out slowly through your mouth or nose for about 6 seconds. A longer out-breath is what settles the body.
Repeat for 5 minutes. If counting makes you tense, just make each out-breath slower than the in-breath.
Notice what has changed: heart rate, shoulders, jaw. Practice daily when calm so it works when you need it.
guides.tip: If you feel dizzy, breathe a little less deeply and slow down rather than forcing big breaths.

guides.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
guides.summary: Pull your attention out of worry and back into the present moment.
steps: Name 5 things you can see. Look around slowly and say them in your head or out loud.
Name 4 things you can feel: your feet on the floor, the chair, your clothes, the air on your skin.
Name 3 things you can hear.
Name 2 things you can smell, or 2 smells you like.
Name 1 thing you can taste, or take one slow sip of water.
Finish with one slow breath and ask: what is actually happening right now?
guides.tip: Grounding is also helpful during flashbacks or when you feel detached.

guides.title: Getting through a panic attack
guides.summary: Panic is intense but not dangerous, and it peaks and passes, usually within minutes.
steps: Remind yourself: this is panic. It is frightening but it will pass. It cannot harm you.
Do not fight it. Fighting the sensations makes them stronger. Let them be there while you do the next steps.
Slow your out-breath (see the breathing guide). Aim for slower, not deeper.
Ground yourself: press your feet into the floor and name 5 things you can see.
Stay where you are if it is safe. Leaving places teaches your brain that the place was dangerous.
Afterwards, rest and be kind to yourself. Note what was happening before it started, which can reveal triggers.
guides.tip: If chest pain is new, severe, or different from your usual panic symptoms, or you are not sure, get medical help. Panic and heart problems can feel alike.

guides.title: Worry time and the worry check
guides.summary: Contain worrying instead of letting it run all day.
steps: Choose a 15-minute 'worry time' each day (not near bedtime).
When a worry appears at other times, jot a few words on a list and tell yourself: I will think about it at worry time.
At worry time, go through the list. For each item ask: Is this something I can act on today? If yes, write one small next step. If no, let it go for now.
Ask: How likely is it, really? What would I tell a friend? How have I coped with similar things before?
When time is up, stop, and do something absorbing: a walk, a call, a task.
guides.tip: Many worries have faded by worry time. Notice that.

guides.title: Facing fears step by step
guides.summary: Avoidance relieves anxiety briefly but strengthens it. Gradual exposure reverses that.
steps: Pick one thing you avoid (for example using public transport, phone calls, social events).
Break it into 8-10 steps from easiest to hardest and rate each from 0-100 for how scary it feels.
Start with a step around 30-40. Stay in it until anxiety drops by about half, or until you've learned the feared outcome did not happen.
Repeat the same step until it feels manageable, then move up.
Don't use safety behaviours (checking, reassurance, escaping) if you can avoid them. They keep the fear alive.
Celebrate each step. Progress is not a straight line.
guides.tip: A therapist trained in CBT can guide this, which is especially helpful for strong phobias, trauma or OCD.

guides.title: Behavioural activation: start small
guides.summary: Doing small things first, even when you feel no desire, gradually lifts mood.
steps: List 10 activities in three groups: things that give pleasure, things that give a sense of achievement, and basic self-care.
Choose 1-2 very small ones for today (for example a 10-minute walk, a shower, one email, hanging laundry).
Put them in your calendar at a specific time.
Do it even if you don't feel like it. Rate your mood 0-10 before and after to see the pattern.
Add one step a few days later. Keep steps small enough that you can succeed on bad days.
Don't judge yourself for missed days. Just start again with the smallest version.
guides.tip: Waiting to feel motivated keeps depression in place. Action is what brings motivation back.

guides.title: A gentle daily routine
guides.summary: A predictable day gives your mind something to hold onto.
steps: Fix a wake-up time and keep it, including weekends (within an hour).
Get daylight within an hour of waking, even a 10-minute walk outside.
Eat something at regular times, even small meals.
Plan one thing with another person each day, such as a message, a call or a coffee.
Plan one thing you can finish each day, however small.
Wind down at a regular time, and keep alcohol low, because it worsens mood and sleep.
guides.tip: Movement of any kind counts. Even gentle exercise a few times per week is linked to better mood.

guides.title: Catching harsh thoughts
guides.summary: Depression makes thoughts sound like facts. A thought record helps you test them.
steps: Write the situation: what happened, where, with whom.
Write the automatic thought (for example 'I'm useless') and how strongly you believe it, 0-100.
Write the feeling and its intensity (sad 80%).
List evidence for the thought and evidence against it. Look for things that don't fit.
Write a more balanced thought, one you'd say to a friend ('I struggled with this task, but I have managed many others').
Re-rate your belief and your feeling. Even a small drop is progress.
guides.tip: If thoughts of ending your life appear, this guide is not enough on its own. Please reach out to a clinician or crisis line today.

guides.title: Reaching out when you'd rather withdraw
guides.summary: Isolation deepens low mood. Small contacts count.
steps: Pick one person who is usually kind and low-pressure.
Send a short, honest message: 'Having a rough patch. Could we talk for 10 minutes this week?' You don't need to explain everything.
If a call feels too much, suggest a walk or doing something together without needing to talk.
If nobody feels safe to contact, consider a peer support line or booking a session with a clinician on MindSight.
Notice how you feel afterwards, usually a bit lighter.
guides.tip: You are not a burden. Most people are glad to be asked.

guides.title: Sleep habits that work
guides.summary: Core habits from CBT for insomnia.
steps: Keep a regular rise time every day. It anchors your body clock more than bedtime.
Only go to bed when sleepy. If you can't sleep after about 20 minutes, get up, do something quiet in dim light, and return when sleepy.
Keep the bed for sleep. No scrolling, working or worrying in bed.
Cut caffeine after midday and avoid alcohol close to bedtime.
Write tomorrow's to-do list earlier in the evening to unload your mind.
Avoid long daytime naps. If you must, limit to 20 minutes before mid-afternoon.
guides.tip: If sleep problems last more than a few weeks or you snore loudly and feel exhausted, talk to a doctor.

guides.title: Recovering from overload
guides.summary: Practical steps when you feel burned out.
steps: List everything on your plate, then mark what must be done, what can wait, and what can be dropped or delegated.
Say no to one thing this week. Notice what actually happens.
Schedule recovery as seriously as work: a daily break with no screens, and one evening per week for yourself.
Move your body gently, and spend time in nature if you can.
Tell your manager or someone close how things really are. Burnout rarely improves without changes to the load.
If you feel exhausted most days for weeks, cynical, or unable to function, see a doctor. A sick leave and treatment may be needed.
guides.tip: Burnout is a signal about the situation, not a personal failing.
